final_method_items.signature: bool gfc_check_assign (gfc_expr *lvalue, gfc_expr *rvalue, int conform, bool allow_convert)
final_method_items.summary: Given an assignable expression and an arbitrary expression, make sure that the assignment can take place. Only add a call to the intrinsic conversion routines, when allow_convert is set. When this assign is a coarray call, then the convert is done by the coarray routine implictly and adding the intrinsic conversion would do harm in most cases.
final_method_items.reason: gfc_check_assign is a very strong candidate because the reproducer’s core bug is that an invalid intrinsic assignment, `z%g = 'x'`, is not rejected during semantic checking and instead survives into lowering, where it later ICEs in allocatable-character assignment code. This function is explicitly responsible for validating whether an assignment is legal, and it already contains special-case rejection logic for illegal procedure-related lhs forms. The suspicious pattern is that it appears to reason mostly from the base symbol (`sym = lvalue->symtree->n.sym`) plus generic refs, but a procedure pointer component like `z%g` is not a plain data object and may evade the existing checks because the base symbol `z` is a derived-type variable while the illegality is in the component designator. That matches the failure mode well: semantic validation misses the bad lhs, translation later misclassifies it, and crashes. While the eventual crash site is in trans-expr.c and a defensive guard may also be needed there, this method is likely the best fix location because the correct behavior is to diagnose and reject the assignment before code generation.

final_method_items.signature: bool gfc_check_vardef_context (gfc_expr* e, bool pointer, bool alloc_obj, bool own_scope, const char* context)
final_method_items.summary: Check if an expression may appear in a variable definition context (F2008, 16.6.7) or pointer association context (F2008, 16.6.8). This is called from the various places when resolving the pieces that make up such a context. If own_scope is true (applies to, e.g., ac-implied-do/data-implied-do variables), some checks are not performed. Optionally, a possible error message can be suppressed if context is NULL and just the return status (true / false) be requested.
final_method_items.reason: gfc_check_vardef_context is a very strong fix candidate because the reproducer should be rejected during semantic checking, before assignment lowering reaches trans-expr.c and crashes. This function is specifically responsible for deciding whether an expression is valid in a variable definition context, which is exactly the role needed for the invalid LHS `z%g` in `z%g = 'x'`. The suspicious details in the body line up closely with the bug: it explicitly handles procedure symbols, pointer/proc-pointer attributes, component references, and even contains a comment noting that normal assignment to procedure pointers is not possible. That makes it highly plausible that a hole here allows a procedure pointer component to be misclassified as a valid assignable object. If this check fails to reject `z%g`, the bad expression can flow into `gfc_trans_assignment_1`, which matches the observed ICE path. I do not give 10 only because the eventual crash is in translation code, so a secondary or alternative fix could also be needed there for robustness; however, as the best semantic fix location, this method is very likely.

final_method_items.summary: Does everything to resolve an ordinary assignment. Returns true if this is an interface assignment.
final_method_items.reason: resolve_ordinary_assign is a very strong fix candidate because the reproducer fails only after the invalid statement `z%g = 'x'` is accepted as an ordinary intrinsic assignment and allowed to proceed into translation. This function is the central resolver for ordinary assignments in `resolve.cc`, so it is exactly where the frontend should reject a procedure pointer component on the LHS before `gfc_trans_assignment_1` and `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment` ever see it. The bug report and stack trace suggest a semantic-classification hole: `z%g` is a procedure pointer component, but assignment resolution treats it like a data object and later allocatable-character logic is triggered by the procedure interface result type. A missing guard here against procedure designators / procedure pointer components as intrinsic-assignment LHS fits the failure well. I do not give 10 only because some of the root mistake could also lie in earlier expression resolution or attribute computation for component references, but among the available candidates this method is one of the most plausible primary fix points.

final_method_items.signature: static tree gfc_trans_assignment_1 (gfc_expr * expr1, gfc_expr * expr2, bool init_flag, bool dealloc, bool use_vptr_copy, bool may_alias)
final_method_items.summary: Subroutine of gfc_trans_assignment that actually scalarizes the assignment. EXPR1 is the destination/LHS and EXPR2 is the source/RHS. init_flag indicates initialization expressions and dealloc that no deallocate prior assignment is needed (if in doubt, set true). When PTR_COPY is set and expr1 is a class type, then use the _vptr-copy routine instead of a pointer assignment. Alias resolution is only done, when MAY_ALIAS is set (the default). This flag is used by ALLOCATE() where it is known, that newly allocated memory on the lhs can never be an alias of the rhs.
final_method_items.reason: `gfc_trans_assignment_1` is a very strong fix location because the ICE occurs directly in its assignment-lowering path, and the backtrace shows this function calling into `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment` for the invalid statement `z%g = 'x'`. The reproducer should have been rejected earlier, since `z%g` is a procedure pointer component, not a data object, but this function is where that bad lhs is still being treated as an ordinary assignable entity. The method also computes `lhs_attr = gfc_expr_attr (expr1)` and makes assignment-mode decisions based on lhs properties, so it is a plausible place where procedure/interface/result-type attributes are being misinterpreted and where a defensive guard against procedure designators could prevent the crash. I do not give 10 because the root cause may originate in earlier semantic resolution/classification that wrongly allows this construct to reach translation at all; in that sense, a more proper fix might live in semantic checking rather than code generation. Still, among candidate locations, this function is one of the strongest because it is exactly where the invalid assignment is lowered into the crashing allocatable-assignment path.

final_method_items.summary: Resolve the interface for a PROCEDURE declaration or procedure pointer.
final_method_items.reason: resolve_procedure_interface is a strong suspect because its job is to propagate interface information from the referenced procedure onto a PROCEDURE symbol, and this reproducer fails exactly when a procedure pointer component to a function returning character(:), allocatable is later mistaken for an assignable allocatable character object. In this function, result attributes and types are copied onto sym, including ts, allocatable, pointer, dimension, result, and character length data. That is very close to the observed failure mode: properties of the function result appear to leak into handling of the procedure pointer component itself. If this routine incorrectly marks the procedure pointer symbol/component with data-object-like attributes, later assignment resolution and translation could wrongly accept z%g = 'x' and route it into allocatable character assignment lowering, causing the ICE. The main reason this is not a 10 is that the actual missing rejection may also belong in semantic assignment checking rather than interface resolution itself; this function may be the enabler rather than the final place where the bug should be fixed.

behavior_items: The reproducer defines a derived type `t` with a procedure pointer component `procedure(f), pointer, nopass :: g`. This means `z%g` is not a character variable or data component; it is a procedure pointer component whose interface matches function `f` and which can later be invoked as `z%g()` if associated.

Function `f` returns `character(:), allocatable`, so a call through the procedure pointer has a deferred-length allocatable character result. That result kind of entity is important because GCC's Fortran frontend has special assignment lowering paths for allocatable character objects and allocatable assignment semantics.

Inside subroutine `s`, the statement `z%g = 'x'` is semantically invalid Fortran. The left-hand side is a procedure pointer component, but the right-hand side is a character literal. A procedure pointer may only participate in valid procedure pointer association contexts, not ordinary intrinsic character assignment.

The following statement `if ( z%g() /= 'abc' ) stop` shows the intended meaning of `g`: it is supposed to be callable like a function returning a string. That confirms that `g` is being treated as a procedure designator elsewhere and that the preceding `z%g = 'x'` is intentionally malformed input exercising compiler diagnostics and robustness, not valid runtime logic.

Older gfortran (shown with gfortran-5) accepts the source and compiles it, which is itself wrong because the invalid assignment should have been rejected. Thus the bug is not a wrong-code runtime bug in valid Fortran but a front-end robustness/diagnostic bug triggered by invalid source.

Newer gfortran versions in the report reach code generation and then crash with an internal compiler error instead of issuing a user-facing semantic error. The backtrace shows the crash happens during translation of the assignment statement, not during parsing.

The stack frame `gfc_trans_assignment_1` indicates the frontend has already classified `z%g = 'x'` as some kind of normal assignment and is attempting to lower it as though the left-hand side were a data object eligible for assignment semantics.

The specific crashing helper `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment` is used when lowering assignments involving scalar allocatable entities, especially deferred-length character assignment where allocation or reallocation of the lhs may be needed. Reaching this helper for `z%g` strongly suggests the compiler is confusing a procedure-pointer component with a character allocatable data object or is reusing lhs metadata that is only valid for data entities.

Because `g`'s target function returns allocatable character, the frontend likely follows type/interface information associated with the procedure pointer and mistakenly reasons about allocatable character assignment properties. In other words, properties of the procedure's result appear to leak into the analysis of the procedure pointer component itself.

That mismatch explains the ICE shape: the compiler expects assignment-related backing data structures for an allocatable scalar lhs, but a procedure pointer component does not have the required representation as an assignable character variable. Dereferencing or querying missing fields then leads to the segmentation fault seen in `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment`.

The bug is therefore exercised entirely at compile time by malformed source that should be diagnosed before lowering. A correct compiler behavior would be to reject `z%g = 'x'` with an error such as assignment to a procedure pointer component not being allowed, and then continue without ICE.

The reproducer is minimal but effective because it combines three ingredients: a procedure pointer component, a function interface returning deferred-length allocatable character, and an intrinsic assignment to that procedure pointer component. That combination drives the frontend down an invalid assignment code path specific to allocatable character handling.

The fact that the report says the regression started with r6 is consistent with this being introduced when procedure pointer components or allocatable character assignment lowering changed, causing invalid lhs forms to survive semantic checking long enough to hit translation code that assumes validity.

No executable behavior is actually required to trigger the bug: compiling with `-c` is sufficient. The `program p` and call to `s` merely ensure the subroutine is instantiated and translated so the faulty assignment statement is processed.

From a compiler-quality perspective, the reproducer tests two things simultaneously: semantic rejection of invalid procedure-pointer assignment, and ICE-resistance in the assignment lowering path when invalid constructs slip through. The observed behavior fails both in newer versions: no proper diagnostic and an internal crash.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The code declares `z%g` as a procedure pointer component whose interface matches a function returning `character(:), allocatable`. The reproducer then performs the invalid statement `z%g = 'x'`, which should be rejected because a procedure pointer is not a character variable and cannot appear as the lhs of intrinsic assignment. Instead, newer gfortran versions mis-handle the statement as if it were an allocatable-character assignment, enter `gfc_trans_assignment_1`, and crash in `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment`. The later `z%g()` call simply confirms that `g` is intended to be callable, highlighting why the assignment is malformed. So the reproducer exercises a front-end semantic-checking hole plus a code-generation ICE caused by confusing a procedure pointer component with the allocatable character result type of its associated function interface.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a front-end robustness regression on invalid Fortran source. The common elements are: (1) the left-hand side `z%g` is a procedure pointer component, not a data object; (2) its declared interface refers to a function returning `character(:), allocatable`; and (3) the invalid statement `z%g = 'x'` is nevertheless propagated into normal assignment lowering. The backtrace shows `gfc_trans_assignment_1` reaching `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment`, which is only appropriate for scalar allocatable data assignment, especially deferred-length character cases. This strongly indicates that semantic analysis failed to reject procedure-pointer intrinsic assignment, and later translation confused properties of the procedure interface/result type with properties of the procedure pointer component itself. The crash is therefore most likely caused by invalid lhs classification plus missing guards/assertions in the Fortran assignment translation path when a non-data entity survives into code generation.
possible_causes: Missing semantic check in the Fortran front end that rejects intrinsic assignment to a procedure pointer component (`EXPR_COMPCALL`/component procedure designator treated as assignable data lhs).

Incorrect lhs classification in assignment resolution/translation, where a procedure pointer component is mis-identified as a scalar character/allocatable variable because the compiler consults the referenced function interface rather than the component's own object category.

Leakage of function result attributes into procedure pointer component handling: the allocatable deferred-length character result of `f` is incorrectly reused when deriving assignment semantics for `z%g`, causing entry into allocatable-character assignment lowering.

Null or invalid metadata dereference in `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment` due to assumptions that the lhs has backing symbol/descriptor fields valid for allocatable data objects, while procedure pointer components do not.

Regression in the Fortran component/procedure-pointer semantic pipeline introduced after r5/r6, allowing invalid procedure-pointer assignments to survive resolution and reach `gfc_trans_assignment_1` without an earlier diagnostic.

Insufficient defensive validation in `gfc_trans_assignment_1` before calling allocatable-assignment helpers; the translator assumes semantic correctness and lacks a guard excluding procedure designators or procedure pointer components from data assignment lowering.
evidence: The bug report explicitly states `z%g =` is invalid, so the source should be rejected semantically rather than lowered.
`z%g` is declared as `procedure(f), pointer, nopass :: g`, which makes it a procedure pointer component, not a character variable or ordinary data component.

The stack trace enters `gfc_trans_assignment_1` and crashes in `alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment`, showing the compiler treated the statement as ordinary assignment and specifically as allocatable-scalar lowering.

`alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment` is associated with allocatable assignment semantics, matching the function result type `character(:), allocatable :: f`; this suggests result-type attributes were confused with lhs object attributes.
The later use `z%g()` confirms `g` is intended as a callable procedure designator, reinforcing that `z%g = 'x'` should never be processed as intrinsic character assignment.
The failure is an ICE during compilation (`-c`), not a runtime issue, which localizes the defect to Fortran front-end semantic resolution and/or translation code rather than the reproducer logic.
Older gfortran accepted the invalid source, while newer versions ICE, indicating a regression where an already-missed diagnostic now additionally reaches a crashing lowering path.

selected_files.reason: The ICE occurs directly in alloc_scalar_allocatable_for_assignment and then gfc_trans_assignment_1, both in this file. The invalid statement z%g = 'x' is being lowered as an allocatable-character assignment, so the primary bug is most likely missing validation or wrong lhs classification in assignment translation here, especially confusion between a procedure pointer component and the allocatable character result type of its interface.

The source is semantically invalid and should have been rejected before translation. This file is the main Fortran semantic resolution layer and is a strong suspect for missing checks that intrinsic assignment lhs must be a data object, not a procedure pointer component. A resolution bug here would explain why invalid code reaches gfc_trans_assignment_1.

Expression construction/classification for procedure designators, component references, and function-related attributes lives here. If the procedure pointer component expression is built or typed in a way that leaks the function result's allocatable character properties onto the lhs expression itself, translation in trans-expr.cc could be misled into the crashing path.

This file handles parsing/matching of member references and assignments. While the crash is later, a parser/matcher issue could incorrectly represent z%g in assignment context as an ordinary variable-like component rather than a procedure pointer designator, enabling the later semantic and translation mistakes.

The problematic case depends on the procedure pointer component having an interface to a function returning character(:), allocatable. Interface handling bugs here could cause result-type attributes of f to be attached or exposed incorrectly when analyzing z%g, contributing to the mistaken allocatable-assignment lowering.

The stack trace passes through trans_code in this file before entering trans-expr.cc. Although likely not the root cause, this dispatcher may lack defensive checks preventing invalid procedure designators from being sent into ordinary assignment lowering.

The crash occurs during function/module code generation, and this file is on the stack via gfc_generate_function_code. It is less likely than trans-expr.cc or resolve.cc, but still potentially involved in preparing symbols/decls or attributes used by assignment translation for procedure pointer components and allocatable character results.

Frontend rewriting/optimization of assignments and expressions happens here. A transformation that normalizes or rewrites the invalid assignment without preserving that the lhs is a procedure pointer component could help route it into the ordinary allocatable-character assignment path.

Given a completely parsed select statement, we: - Validate all expressions and code within the SELECT. - Make sure that the selection expression is not of the wrong type. - Make sure that no case ranges overlap. - Eliminate unreachable cases and unreachable code resulting from removing case labels. The standard does allow unreachable cases, e.g. CASE (5:3). But they are a hassle for code generation, and to prevent that, we just cut them out here. This is not necessary for overlapping cases because they are illegal and we never even try to generate code. We have the additional caveat that a SELECT construct could have been a computed GOTO in the source code. Fortunately we can fairly easily work around that here: The case_expr for a "real" SELECT CASE is in code->expr1, but for a computed GOTO it is in code->expr2. All we have to do is make sure that the case_expr is a scalar integer expression.

We work by recursively simplifying expression nodes, simplifying intrinsic functions where possible, which can lead to further constant collapsing. If an operator has constant operand(s), we rip the expression apart, and rebuild it, hoping that it becomes something simpler. The expression type is defined for: 0 Basic expression parsing 1 Simplifying array constructors -- will substitute iterator values. Returns false on error, true otherwise. NOTE: Will return true even if the expression cannot be simplified.
Try simplification of an expression via gfc_simplify_expr. When an error occurs (arithmetic or otherwise), roll back.
Returns the type of an expression with the exception that iterator variables are automatically integers no matter what else they may be declared as.
Scalarize an expression for an elemental intrinsic call.
F2003, 7.1.7 (3): In init expression, allocatable components must not be data-initialized.
F95, 7.1.6.1, Initialization expressions, (7) F2003, 7.1.7 Initialization expression, (8) F2008, 7.1.12 Constant expression, (4)
F95, 7.1.6.1, Initialization expressions, (5) F2003, 7.1.7 Initialization expression, (5)
F95, 7.1.6.1, Initialization expressions, (6) F2003, 7.1.7 Initialization expression, (6)

Verify that an expression is an initialization expression. A side effect is that the expression tree is reduced to a single constant node if all goes well. This would normally happen when the expression is constructed but function references are assumed to be intrinsics in the context of initialization expressions. If false is returned an error message has been generated.
Reduces a general expression to an initialization expression (a constant). This used to be part of gfc_match_init_expr. Note that this function doesn't free the given expression on false.
Match an initialization expression. We work by first matching an expression, then reducing it to a constant.
Given an actual argument list, test to see that each argument is a restricted expression and optionally if the expression type is integer or character.
Make sure a non-intrinsic function is a specification function, see F08:7.1.11.5.
Check to see that a function reference to an intrinsic is a restricted expression.
Check the expressions of an actual arglist. Used by check_restricted.
Check the subscription expressions of a reference chain with a checking function; used by check_restricted.
Return true if ns is a parent of the current ns.
Verify that an expression is a restricted expression. Like its cousin check_init_expr(), an error message is generated if we return false.
Check to see that an expression is a specification expression. If we return false, an error has been generated.
Given two expressions, make sure that the arrays are conformable.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_assign (gfc_expr *lvalue, gfc_expr *rvalue, int conform, bool allow_convert)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Given an assignable expression and an arbitrary expression, make sure that the assignment can take place. Only add a call to the intrinsic conversion routines, when allow_convert is set. When this assign is a coarray call, then the convert is done by the coarray routine implictly and adding the intrinsic conversion would do harm in most cases.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_pointer_assign (gfc_expr *lvalue, gfc_expr *rvalue, bool suppress_type_test, bool is_init_expr)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Check that a pointer assignment is OK. We first check lvalue, and we only check rvalue if it's not an assignment to NULL() or a NULLIFY statement.
Relative of gfc_check_assign() except that the lvalue is a single symbol. Used for initialization assignments.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: static gfc_expr * gfc_build_init_expr (gfc_typespec *ts, locus *where, bool force)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Build an initializer for a local integer, real, complex, logical, or character variable, based on the command line flags finit-local-zero, finit-integer=, finit-real=, finit-logical=, and finit-character=. With force, an initializer is ALWAYS generated.
Invoke gfc_build_init_expr to create an initializer expression, but do not require that an expression be built.
Apply an initialization expression to a typespec. Can be used for symbols or components. Similar to add_init_expr_to_sym in decl.cc; could probably be combined with some effort.
Check whether an expression is a structure constructor and whether it has other values than NULL.
Check for default initializer; sym->value is not enough as it is also set for EXPR_NULL of allocatables.

Generate an initializer expression which initializes the entirety of a union. A normal structure constructor is insufficient without undue effort, because components of maps may be oddly aligned/overlapped. (For example if a character is initialized from one map overtop a real from the other, only one byte of the real is actually initialized.) Unfortunately we don't know the size of the union right now, so we can't generate a proper initializer, but we use a NULL expr as a placeholder and do the right thing later in gfc_trans_subcomponent_assign.

Get the user-specified initializer for a union, if any. This means the user has said to initialize component(s) of a map. For simplicity's sake we only allow the user to initialize the first map. We don't have to worry about overlapping initializers as they are released early in resolution (see resolve_fl_struct).
Fetch or generate an initializer for the given component. Only generate an initializer if generate is true.
Get an expression for a default initializer of a derived type.
Generate an initializer expression for an iso_c_binding type such as c_[fun]ptr. The appropriate initializer is c_null_[fun]ptr.

Get or generate an expression for a default initializer of a derived type. If -finit-derived is specified, generate default initialization expressions for components that lack them when generate is set.
Given a symbol, create an expression node with that symbol as a variable. If the symbol is array valued, setup a reference of the whole array.
Adds a full array reference to an expression, as needed.
Returns the array_spec of a full array expression. A NULL is returned otherwise.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: General expression traversal function.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: static bool expr_set_symbols_referenced (gfc_expr *expr, gfc_symbol *sym ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, int *f ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Traverse expr, marking all EXPR_VARIABLE symbols referenced.
Determine if an expression is a procedure pointer component and return the component in that case. Otherwise return NULL.
Determine if an expression is a procedure pointer component.
Determine if an expression is a function with an allocatable class scalar result.
Determine if an expression is a function with an allocatable class array result.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: static bool expr_check_typed_help (gfc_expr* e, gfc_symbol* sym ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, int* f ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
bool gfc_expr_check_typed (gfc_expr* e, gfc_namespace* ns, bool strict)
static bool derived_parameter_expr (gfc_expr* e, gfc_symbol* sym ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, int* f ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: This function returns true if it contains any references to PDT KIND or LEN parameters.

This function returns the overall type of a type parameter spec list. If all the specs are explicit, SPEC_EXPLICIT is returned. If any of the parameters are assumed/deferred then SPEC_ASSUMED/DEFERRED is returned unless derived is not NULL. In this latter case, all the LEN parameters must be either assumed or deferred for the return argument to be set to anything other than SPEC_EXPLICIT.

Coarrays are variables with a corank but not being coindexed. However, also the following is a coarray: A subobject of a coarray is a coarray if it does not have any cosubscripts, vector subscripts, allocatable component selection, or pointer component selection. (F2008, 2.4.7)
Check whether the expression has an ultimate allocatable component. Being itself allocatable does not count.
Check whether the expression has an pointer component. Being itself a pointer does not count.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: bool gfc_is_simply_contiguous (gfc_expr *expr, bool strict, bool permit_element)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Check whether an expression is "simply contiguous", cf. F2008, 6.5.4. Note: A scalar is not regarded as "simply contiguous" by the standard. if bool is not strict, some further checks are done - for instance, a "(::1)" is accepted.

Return true if the expression is guaranteed to be non-contiguous, false if we cannot prove anything. It is probably best to call this after gfc_is_simply_contiguous. If neither of them returns true, we cannot say (at compile-time).

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: gfc_expr* gfc_build_intrinsic_call (gfc_namespace *ns, gfc_isym_id id, const char* name, locus where, unsigned numarg, ...)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Build call to an intrinsic procedure. The number of arguments has to be passed (rather than ending the list with a NULL value) because we may want to add arguments but with a NULL-expression.

gcc/fortran/expr.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_vardef_context (gfc_expr* e, bool pointer, bool alloc_obj, bool own_scope, const char* context)
gcc/fortran/expr.cc.summary: Check if an expression may appear in a variable definition context (F2008, 16.6.7) or pointer association context (F2008, 16.6.8). This is called from the various places when resolving the pieces that make up such a context. If own_scope is true (applies to, e.g., ac-implied-do/data-implied-do variables), some checks are not performed. Optionally, a possible error message can be suppressed if context is NULL and just the return status (true / false) be requested.

gcc/fortran/match.cc.summary: For debugging and diagnostic purposes. Return the textual representation of the intrinsic operator OP.

Matches a member separator. With standard FORTRAN this is '%', but with DEC structures we must carefully match dot ('.'). Because operators are spelled ".op.", a dotted string such as "x.y.z..." can be either a component reference chain or a combination of binary operations. There is no real way to win because the string may be grammatically ambiguous. The following rules help avoid ambiguities - they match some behavior of other (older) compilers. If the rules here are changed the test cases should be updated. If the user has problems with these rules they probably deserve the consequences. Consider "x.y.z": (1) If any user defined operator ".y." exists, this is always y(x,z) (even if ".y." is the wrong type and/or x has a member y). (2) Otherwise if x has a member y, and y is itself a derived type, this is (x->y)->z, even if an intrinsic operator exists which can handle (x,z). (3) If x has no member y or (x->y) is not a derived type but ".y." is an intrinsic operator (such as ".eq."), this is y(x,z). (4) Lastly if there is no operator ".y." and x has no member "y", it is an error. It is worth noting that the logic here does not support mixed use of member accessors within a singl
This function scans the current statement counting the opened and closed parenthesis to make sure they are balanced.
See if the next character is a special character that has escaped by a \ via the -fbackslash option.
In free form, match at least one space. Always matches in fixed form.
Match an end of statement. End of statement is optional whitespace, followed by a ';' or '\n' or comment '!'. If a semicolon is found, we continue to eat whitespace and semicolons.

Match a literal integer on the input, setting the value on MATCH_YES. Literal ints occur in kind-parameters as well as old-style character length specifications. If cnt is non-NULL it will be set to the number of digits. When gobble_ws is false, do not skip over leading blanks.
Match a small, constant integer expression, like in a kind statement. On MATCH_YES, 'value' is set.
Matches a statement label. Uses gfc_match_small_literal_int() to do most of the work.

Match and validate a label associated with a named IF, DO or SELECT statement. If the symbol does not have the label attribute, we add it. We also make sure the symbol does not refer to another (active) block. A matched label is pointed to by gfc_new_block.

See if the current input looks like a name of some sort. Modifies the passed buffer which must be GFC_MAX_SYMBOL_LEN+1 bytes long. Note that options.cc restricts max_identifier_length to not more than GFC_MAX_SYMBOL_LEN. When gobble_ws is false, do not skip over leading blanks.
Match a symbol on the input. Modifies the pointer to the symbol pointer if successful.
Match an intrinsic operator. Returns an INTRINSIC enum. While matching, we always find INTRINSIC_PLUS before INTRINSIC_UPLUS. We work around this in matchexp.cc.

Match a loop control phrase: <LVALUE> = <EXPR>, <EXPR> [, <EXPR> ] If the final integer expression is not present, a constant unity expression is returned. We don't return MATCH_ERROR until after the equals sign is seen.
Tries to match the next non-whitespace character on the input. This subroutine does not return MATCH_ERROR. When gobble_ws is false, do not skip over leading blanks.

General purpose matching subroutine. The target string is a scanf-like format string in which spaces correspond to arbitrary whitespace (including no whitespace), characters correspond to themselves. The %-codes are: %% Literal percent sign %e Expression, pointer to a pointer is set %s Symbol, pointer to the symbol is set %n Name, character buffer is set to name %t Matches end of statement. %o Matches an intrinsic operator, returned as an INTRINSIC enum. %l Matches a statement label %v Matches a variable expression (an lvalue, except function references having a data pointer result) % Matches a required space (in free form) and optional spaces.
Matches the start of a program unit, which is the program keyword followed by an obligatory symbol.
Match a simple assignment statement.
Match a pointer assignment statement.

We try to match an easy arithmetic IF statement. This only happens when just after having encountered a simple IF statement. This code is really duplicate with parts of the gfc_match_if code, but this is much* easier.
Match an ELSE statement.
Match an ELSE IF statement.
Free a gfc_iterator structure.
Match a CRITICAL statement.
Match a BLOCK statement.
Match an ASSOCIATE statement.
Match a Fortran 2003 derived-type-spec (F03:R455), which is just the name of an accessible derived type.

Match a Fortran 2003 type-spec (F03:R401). This is similar to gfc_match_decl_type_spec() from decl.cc, with the following exceptions: It only includes the intrinsic types from the Fortran 2003 standard (thus, neither BYTE nor forms like REAL*4 are allowed). Additionally, the implicit_flag is not needed, so it was removed. Derived types are identified by their name alone.
Free a list of FORALL iterators.
Match an iterator as part of a FORALL statement. The format is: <var> = <start>:<end>[:<stride>] On MATCH_NO, the caller tests for the possibility that there is a scalar mask expression.
Match the header of a FORALL statement.
Match the rest of a simple FORALL statement that follows an IF statement.
Match a FORALL statement.
Match a DO statement.

gcc/fortran/match.cc.signature: static match match_exit_cycle (gfc_statement st, gfc_exec_op op)
gcc/fortran/match.cc.summary: Match an EXIT or CYCLE statement.
Match the EXIT statement.
Match the CYCLE statement.

Match a stop-code after an (ERROR) STOP or PAUSE statement. The requirements for a stop-code differ in the standards. Fortran 95 has R840 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R841 stop-code is scalar-char-constant or digit [ digit [ digit [ digit [ digit ] ] ] ] Fortran 2003 matches Fortran 95 except R840 and R841 are now R849 and R850. Fortran 2008 has R855 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R856 allstop-stmt is ALL STOP [ stop-code ] R857 stop-code is scalar-default-char-constant-expr or scalar-int-constant-expr Fortran 2018 has R1160 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1161 error-stop-stmt is ERROR STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1162 stop-code is scalar-default-char-expr or scalar-int-expr For free-form source code, all standards contain a statement of the form: A blank shall be used to separate names, constants, or labels from adjacent keywords, names, constants, or labels. A stop-code is not a name, constant, or label. So, under Fortran 95 and 2003, STOP123 is valid, but it is invalid Fortran 2008.
Match the (deprecated) PAUSE statement.
Match the STOP statement.
Match the ERROR STOP statement.

Match EVENT POST/WAIT statement. Syntax: EVENT POST ( event-variable [, sync-stat-list] ) EVENT WAIT ( event-variable [, wait-spec-list] ) with wait-spec-list is sync-stat-list or until-spec until-spec is UNTIL_COUNT = scalar-int-expr sync-stat is STAT= or ERRMSG=.
Match a FAIL IMAGE statement.
Match a FORM TEAM statement.
Match a CHANGE TEAM statement.
Match a END TEAM statement.
Match a SYNC TEAM statement.

Match LOCK/UNLOCK statement. Syntax: LOCK ( lock-variable [ , lock-stat-list ] ) UNLOCK ( lock-variable [ , sync-stat-list ] ) where lock-stat is ACQUIRED_LOCK or sync-stat and sync-stat is STAT= or ERRMSG=.
Match SYNC ALL/IMAGES/MEMORY statement. Syntax: SYNC ALL [(sync-stat-list)] SYNC MEMORY [(sync-stat-list)] SYNC IMAGES (image-set [, sync-stat-list] ) with sync-stat is int-expr or *.
Match SYNC ALL statement.
Match SYNC IMAGES statement.
Match SYNC MEMORY statement.
Match a CONTINUE statement.
Match the (deprecated) ASSIGN statement.

Match the GO TO statement. As a computed GOTO statement is matched, it is transformed into an equivalent SELECT block. No tree is necessary, and the resulting jumps-to-jumps are specifically optimized away by the back end.
Frees a list of gfc_alloc structures.
Match an ALLOCATE statement.
Match a NULLIFY statement. A NULLIFY statement is transformed into a set of pointer assignments to intrinsic NULL().
Match a DEALLOCATE statement.
Match a RETURN statement.
Match the call of a type-bound procedure, if CALL%var has already been matched and var found to be a derived-type variable.

Match a CALL statement. The tricky part here are possible alternate return specifiers. We handle these by having all "subroutines" actually return an integer via a register that gives the return number. If the call specifies alternate returns, we generate code for a SELECT statement whose case clauses contain GOTOs to the various labels.

Given a name, return a pointer to the common head structure, creating it if it does not exist. If FROM_MODULE is nonzero, we mangle the name so that it doesn't interfere with commons defined in the using namespace. TODO: Add to global symbol tree.
Match a common block name.
Match a COMMON statement.
Match a BLOCK DATA program unit.
Free a namelist structure.

Match a NAMELIST statement.
Match a MODULE statement.
Free equivalence sets and lists. Recursively is the easiest way to do this.
Match an EQUIVALENCE statement.

Match an assignment to a pointer function (F2008). This could, in general be ambiguous with a statement function. In this implementation it remains so if it is the first statement after the specification block.
Free a single case structure.
Free a list of case structures.
Match a single case selector. Combining the requirements of F08:C830 and F08:C832 (R838) means that the case-value must have either CHARACTER, INTEGER, or LOGICAL type.
Match the end of a case statement.
Match a SELECT statement.
Transfer the selector typespec to the associate name.
Push the current selector onto the SELECT TYPE stack.
Set the temporary for the current intrinsic SELECT TYPE selector.
Set up a temporary for the current TYPE IS / CLASS IS branch .
Match a SELECT TYPE statement.
Set the temporary for the current intrinsic SELECT RANK selector.
Match a SELECT RANK statement.
Match a CASE statement.
Match a TYPE IS statement.
Match a CLASS IS or CLASS DEFAULT statement.
Match a RANK statement.
Match the rest of a simple WHERE statement that follows an IF statement.
Match a WHERE statement.
Match an ELSEWHERE statement. We leave behind a WHERE node in new_st if successful.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Free a singly linked list of gfc_interface structures.
Change the operators unary plus and minus into binary plus and minus respectively, leaving the rest unchanged.
Return the operator depending on the DTIO moded string. Note that these are not operators in the normal sense and so have been placed beyond GFC_INTRINSIC_END in gfortran.h:enum gfc_intrinsic_op.
Match a generic specification. Depending on which type of interface is found, the 'name' or 'op' pointers may be set. This subroutine doesn't return MATCH_NO.
Match one of the five F95 forms of an interface statement. The matcher for the abstract interface follows.
Match a F2003 abstract interface.
Match the different sort of generic-specs that can be present after the END INTERFACE itself.
Return whether the component was defined anonymously.
Return whether the derived type was defined anonymously.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static bool compare_components (gfc_component *cmp1, gfc_component *cmp2, gfc_symbol *derived1, gfc_symbol *derived2)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Compare components according to 4.4.2 of the Fortran standard.

Compare two union types by comparing the components of their maps. Because unions and maps are anonymous their types get special internal names; therefore the usual derived type comparison will fail on them. Returns nonzero if equal, as with gfc_compare_derived_types. Also as with gfc_compare_derived_types, 'equal' is closer to meaning 'duplicate definitions' than 'equivalent structure'.
Compare two derived types using the criteria in 4.4.2 of the standard, recursing through gfc_compare_types for the components.
Compare two typespecs, recursively if necessary.
Given two symbols that are formal arguments, compare their ranks and types. Returns true if they have the same rank and type, false otherwise.
Given two symbols that are formal arguments, compare their types and rank and their formal interfaces if they are both dummy procedures. Returns true if the same, false if different.
Given a formal argument list and a keyword name, search the list for that keyword. Returns the correct symbol node if found, NULL if not found.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_operator_interface (gfc_symbol *sym, gfc_intrinsic_op op, locus opwhere)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Given an operator interface and the operator, make sure that all interfaces for that operator are legal.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static bool count_types_test (gfc_formal_arglist *f1, gfc_formal_arglist *f2, const char *p1, const char *p2)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Given a pair of formal argument lists, we see if the two lists can be distinguished by counting the number of nonoptional arguments of a given type/rank in f1 and seeing if there are less then that number of those arguments in f2 (including optional arguments). Since this test is asymmetric, it has to be called twice to make it symmetric. Returns nonzero if the argument lists are incompatible by this test. This subroutine implements rule 1 of section F03:16.2.3. 'p1' and 'p2' are the PASS arguments of both procedures (if applicable).

Returns true if two dummy arguments are distinguishable due to their POINTER and ALLOCATABLE attributes according to F2018 section 15.4.3.4.5 (3). The function is asymmetric wrt to the arguments s1 and s2 and should always be called twice (with flipped arguments in the second call).

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static bool generic_correspondence (gfc_formal_arglist *f1, gfc_formal_arglist *f2, const char *p1, const char *p2)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Perform the correspondence test in rule (3) of F08:C1215. Returns zero if no argument is found that satisfies this rule, nonzero otherwise. 'p1' and 'p2' are the PASS arguments of both procedures (if applicable). This test is also not symmetric in f1 and f2 and must be called twice. This test finds problems caused by sorting the actual argument list with keywords. For example: INTERFACE FOO SUBROUTINE F1(A, B) INTEGER :: A ; REAL :: B END SUBROUTINE F1 SUBROUTINE F2(B, A) INTEGER :: A ; REAL :: B END SUBROUTINE F1 END INTERFACE FOO At this point, 'CALL FOO(A=1, B=1.0)' is ambiguous.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_dummy_characteristics (gfc_symbol *s1, gfc_symbol *s2, bool type_must_agree, char *errmsg, int err_len)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Check if the characteristics of two dummy arguments match, cf. F08:12.3.2.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: bool gfc_check_result_characteristics (gfc_symbol *s1, gfc_symbol *s2, char *errmsg, int err_len)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Check if the characteristics of two function results match, cf. F08:12.3.3.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: bool gfc_compare_interfaces (gfc_symbol *s1, gfc_symbol *s2, const char *name2, int generic_flag, int strict_flag, char *errmsg, int err_len, const char *p1, const char *p2, bool *bad_result_characteristics)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: 'Compare' two formal interfaces associated with a pair of symbols. We return true if there exists an actual argument list that would be ambiguous between the two interfaces, zero otherwise. 'strict_flag' specifies whether all the characteristics are required to match, which is not the case for ambiguity checks. 'p1' and 'p2' are the PASS arguments of both procedures (if applicable).

Given a pointer to an interface pointer, remove duplicate interfaces and make sure that all symbols are either functions or subroutines, and all of the same kind. Returns true if something goes wrong.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static bool check_interface1 (gfc_interface *p, gfc_interface *q0, int generic_flag, const char *interface_name, bool referenced)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Check lists of interfaces to make sure that no two interfaces are ambiguous. Duplicate interfaces (from the same symbol) are OK here.
Check the generic and operator interfaces of symbols to make sure that none of the interfaces conflict. The check has to be done after all of the symbols are actually loaded.
Given an intrinsic op, return an equivalent op if one exists, or INTRINSIC_NONE otherwise.

For the namespace, check generic, user operator and intrinsic operator interfaces for consistency and to remove duplicate interfaces. We traverse the whole namespace, counting on the fact that most symbols will not have generic or operator interfaces.
Given a symbol of a formal argument list and an expression, if the formal argument is allocatable, check that the actual argument is allocatable. Returns true if compatible, zero if not compatible.
Given a symbol of a formal argument list and an expression, if the formal argument is a pointer, see if the actual argument is a pointer. Returns nonzero if compatible, zero if not compatible.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static void argument_rank_mismatch (const char *name, locus *where, int rank1, int rank2, locus *where_formal)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Emit clear error messages for rank mismatch.

Under certain conditions, a scalar actual argument can be passed to an array dummy argument - see F2018, 15.5.2.4, paragraph 14. This function returns true for these conditions so that an error or warning for this can be suppressed later. Always return false for expressions with rank > 0.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static bool compare_parameter (gfc_symbol *formal, gfc_expr *actual, int ranks_must_agree, int is_elemental, locus *where)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Given a symbol of a formal argument list and an expression, see if the two are compatible as arguments. Returns true if compatible, false if not compatible.
Returns the storage size of a symbol (formal argument) or zero if it cannot be determined.

Returns the storage size of an expression (actual argument) or zero if it cannot be determined. For an array element, it returns the remaining size as the element sequence consists of all storage units of the actual argument up to the end of the array.
Given an expression, check whether it is an array section which has a vector subscript.
Recursively append candidate argument ARG to CANDIDATES. Store the number of total candidates in CANDIDATES_LEN.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static const char* lookup_arg_fuzzy (const char *arg, gfc_formal_arglist *arguments)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Lookup argument ARG fuzzily, taking names in ARGUMENTS into account.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: bool gfc_compare_actual_formal (gfc_actual_arglist **ap, gfc_formal_arglist *formal, int ranks_must_agree, int is_elemental, bool in_statement_function, locus *where)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: Given formal and actual argument lists, see if they are compatible. If they are compatible, the actual argument list is sorted to correspond with the formal list, and elements for missing optional arguments are inserted. If WHERE pointer is nonnull, then we issue errors when things don't match instead of just returning the status code.

gcc/fortran/interface.cc.signature: static int pair_cmp (const void *p1, const void *p2)
gcc/fortran/interface.cc.summary: qsort comparison function for argument pairs, with the following order: - p->a->expr == NULL - p->a->expr->expr_type != EXPR_VARIABLE - by gfc_symbol pointer value (larger first).

gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.summary: Implement TARGET_IRA_CHANGE_PSEUDO_ALLOCNO_CLASS. The register allocator chooses POINTER_AND_FP_REGS if FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS have the same cost - even if POINTER_AND_FP_REGS has a much higher cost. POINTER_AND_FP_REGS is also used if the cost of both FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS is lower than the memory cost (in this case the best class is the lowest cost one). Using POINTER_AND_FP_REGS irrespectively of its cost results in bad allocations with many redundant int<->FP moves which are expensive on various cores. To avoid this we don't allow POINTER_AND_FP_REGS as the allocno class, but force a decision between FP_REGS and GENERAL_REGS. We use the allocno class if it isn't POINTER_AND_FP_REGS. Similarly, use the best class if it isn't POINTER_AND_FP_REGS. Otherwise set the allocno class depending on the mode. The result of this is that it is no longer inefficient to have a higher memory move cost than the register move cost.

PRED_MODE is the mode of the predicate. See the comment at the head of aarch64-sve.md for details about the big-endian handling.

See whether an SVE vector move from SRC to DEST is effectively a REV[BHW] instruction, because at least one operand is a subreg of an SVE vector that has wider or narrower elements. Return true and emit the instruction if so. For example: (set (reg:VNx8HI R1) (subreg:VNx8HI (reg:VNx16QI R2) 0)) represents a VIEW_CONVERT between the following vectors, viewed in memory order: R2: { [0].high, [0].low, [1].high, [1].low, ... } R1: { [0], [1], [2], [3], ... } The high part of lane X in R2 should therefore correspond to lane X*2 of R1, but the register representations are: msb lsb R2: ...... [1].high [1].low [0].high [0].low R1: ...... [3] [2] [1] [0] where the low part of lane X in R2 corresponds to lane X*2 in R1. We therefore need a reverse operation to swap the high and low values around. This is purely an optimization. Without it we would spill the subreg operand to the stack in one mode and reload it in the other mode, which has the same effect as the REV.

gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.summary: Print operand X to file F in a target specific manner according to CODE. The acceptable formatting commands given by CODE are: 'c': An integer or symbol address without a preceding # sign. 'C': Take the duplicated element in a vector constant and print it in hex. 'D': Take the duplicated element in a vector constant and print it as an unsigned integer, in decimal. 'e': Print the sign/zero-extend size as a character 8->b, 16->h, 32->w. Can also be used for masks: 0xff->b, 0xffff->h, 0xffffffff->w. 'I': If the operand is a duplicated vector constant, replace it with the duplicated scalar. If the operand is then a floating-point constant, replace it with the integer bit representation. Print the transformed constant as a signed decimal number. 'p': Prints N such that 2^N == X (X must be power of 2 and const int). 'P': Print the number of non-zero bits in X (a const_int). 'H': Print the higher numbered register of a pair (TImode) of regs. 'm': Print a condition (eq, ne, etc). 'M': Same as 'm', but invert condition. 'N': Take the duplicated element in a vector constant and print the negative of it in decimal. 'b/h/s/d/q': Print a scalar FP/SIMD register name. 'S/T/U/V': Print a FP/SIMD

gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.signature: static int aapcs_vfp_sub_candidate (const_tree type, machine_mode *modep, unsigned int *warn_psabi_flags)
gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.summary: Walk down the type tree of TYPE counting consecutive base elements. If *MODEP is VOIDmode, then set it to the first valid floating point type. If a non-floating point type is found, or if a floating point type that doesn't match a non-VOIDmode *MODEP is found, then return -1, otherwise return the count in the sub-tree. The WARN_PSABI_FLAGS argument allows the caller to check whether this function has changed its behavior relative to earlier versions of GCC. Normally the argument should be nonnull and point to a zero-initialized variable. The function then records whether the ABI decision might be affected by a known fix to the ABI logic, setting the associated WARN_PSABI_* bits if so. When the argument is instead a null pointer, the function tries to simulate the behavior of GCC before all such ABI fixes were made. This is useful to check whether the function returns something different after the ABI fixes.

gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.signature: static bool aarch64_composite_type_p (const_tree type, machine_mode mode)
gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.summary: Return TRUE if the type, as described by TYPE and MODE, is a composite type as described in AAPCS64 \S 4.3. This includes aggregate, union and array types. The C99 floating-point complex types are also considered as composite types, according to AAPCS64 \S 7.1.1. The complex integer types, which are GCC extensions and out of the scope of AAPCS64, are treated as composite types here as well. Note that MODE itself is not sufficient in determining whether a type is such a composite type or not. This is because stor-layout.cc:compute_record_mode may have already changed the MODE (BLKmode) of a RECORD_TYPE TYPE to some other mode. For example, a structure with only one field may have its MODE set to the mode of the field. Also an integer mode whose size matches the size of the RECORD_TYPE type may be used to substitute the original mode (i.e. BLKmode) in certain circumstances. In other words, MODE cannot be solely relied on.

This does not line up with GCC's perspective on lane numbers, so we end up with different masks depending on our target endian-ness. The diagram below may help. We must draw the distinction when building masks which select one half of the vector. An instruction selecting architectural low-lanes for a big-endian target, must be described using a mask selecting GCC high-lanes. Big-Endian Little-Endian GCC 0 1 2 3 3 2 1 0 | x | x | x | x | | x | x | x | x | Architecture 3 2 1 0 3 2 1 0 Low Mask: { 2, 3 } { 0, 1 } High Mask: { 0, 1 } { 2, 3 } MODE Is the mode of the vector and NUNITS is the number of units in it.

gcc/config/aarch64/aarch64.cc.summary: Initialize register TARGET from BUILDER. NELTS is the constant number of elements in BUILDER. The function tries to initialize TARGET from BUILDER if it fits one of the special cases outlined below. Failing that, the function divides BUILDER into two sub-vectors: v_even = even elements of BUILDER; v_odd = odd elements of BUILDER; and recursively calls itself with v_even and v_odd. if (recursive call succeeded for v_even or v_odd) TARGET = zip (v_even, v_odd) The function returns true if it managed to build TARGET from BUILDER with one of the special cases, false otherwise. Example: {a, 1, b, 2, c, 3, d, 4} The vector gets divided into: v_even = {a, b, c, d} v_odd = {1, 2, 3, 4} aarch64_sve_expand_vector_init(v_odd) hits case 1 and initialize tmp2 from constant vector v_odd using emit_move_insn. aarch64_sve_expand_vector_init(v_even) fails since v_even contains 4 elements, so we construct tmp1 from v_even using insr: tmp1 = dup(d) insr tmp1, c insr tmp1, b insr tmp1, a And finally: TARGET = zip (tmp1, tmp2) which sets TARGET to {a, 1, b, 2, c, 3, d, 4}.

The likely estimate is the same as the minimum in that case to give a conservative behavior of auto-vectorizing with SVE when it is a win even for 128-bit SVE. When SVE width information is available VAL.coeffs[1] is multiplied by the number of VQ chunks over the initial Advanced SIMD 128 bits.

Helper function for straight line speculation. Return what barrier should be emitted for straight line speculation mitigation. When not mitigating against straight line speculation this function returns an empty string. When mitigating against straight line speculation, use: SB when the v8.5-A SB extension is enabled. DSB+ISB otherwise.

Function to create a BLR thunk. This thunk is used to mitigate straight line speculation. Instead of a simple BLR that can be speculated past, we emit a BL to this thunk, and this thunk contains a BR to the relevant register. These thunks have the relevant speculation barries put after their indirect branch so that speculation is blocked. We use such a thunk so the speculation barriers are kept off the architecturally executed path in order to reduce the performance overhead. When optimizing for size we use stubs shared by the linked object. When optimizing for performance we emit stubs for each function in the hope that the branch predictor can better train on jumps specific for a given function.
Helper function for aarch64_sls_emit_blr_function_thunks and aarch64_sls_emit_shared_blr_thunks below.

Emit all BLR stubs for this particular function. Here we emit all the BLR stubs needed for the current function. Since we emit these stubs in a consecutive block we know there will be no speculation gadgets between each stub, and hence we only emit a speculation barrier at the end of the stub sequences. This is called in the TARGET_ASM_FUNCTION_EPILOGUE hook.

Emit shared BLR stubs for the current compilation unit. Over the course of compiling this unit we may have converted some BLR instructions to a BL to a shared stub function. This is where we emit those stub functions. This function is for the stubs shared between different functions in this compilation unit. We share when optimizing for size instead of speed. This function is called through the TARGET_ASM_FILE_END hook.
Implement TARGET_ASM_FILE_END.
